blocks.text: You can count the number of pages of a book exactly, but measuring its length needs a measuring instrument. Every instrument is calibrated to a certain smallest division mark, and this fact puts a limit on its accuracy: when you take a reading with an instrument, its limit of measurement is the smallest division or graduation on its scale. Hence every measured quantity has some uncertainty about its value. When a measurement is made it is taken to the nearest graduation or marking on the scale, and the maximum uncertainty can be estimated as one smallest division of the instrument.

blocks.title: Absolute uncertainty
blocks.text: The maximum uncertainty in a reading, estimated as one smallest division of the instrument, is the absolute uncertainty. It is one millimetre on a metre rule graduated in millimetres.

For example, if one edge of a book coincides with the 10.0 cm mark and the other with 33.5 cm, the length with its uncertainty is (33.5 +/- 0.05) cm - (10.0 +/- 0.05) cm = (23.5 +/- 0.1) cm. The true length of the book is between 23.4 cm and 23.6 cm; the maximum uncertainty is +/-0.05 cm at each end, equivalent to an uncertainty of 0.1 cm in the length, which equals the least count of the metre rule.

blocks.title: Fractional and percentage uncertainty
blocks.text: Fractional uncertainty = absolute uncertainty / measured value. Percentage uncertainty = (absolute uncertainty / measured value) x 100.

Some modern measuring instruments have a digital scale. We usually estimate one digit beyond what is certain; with a digital scale this is reflected in some fluctuation of the last digit. If the last digit fluctuates by 1 or 2, write down that last digit. If the fluctuation is more than 2 or so in the last digit, the reading is being influenced by some factor such as air currents; regardless of the reason, a large fluctuation may mean that the displayed digit is not really significant. The indication of uncertainty in a recorded value has been simplified using significant figures: if a measurement is recorded with the knowledge of significant figures, its last digit, which is an estimation, indicates the accuracy of the recorded value.

blocks.prompt: A digital balance shows 24.36 g, 24.37 g, 24.36 g on successive readings, and a second one shows 24.3, 24.9, 24.1 g. What should be recorded in each case?
blocks.explanation: The first display fluctuates by only 1 in the last digit, so the last digit is kept: 24.36 g (or 24.37 g) with an uncertainty of about 0.01 g. The second fluctuates by much more than 2 in the last digit, so something such as air currents is disturbing it and the last digit is not significant; the reading should be given as 24 g, or the cause removed before recording.

items: Every instrument reads to its smallest division; the absolute uncertainty is one least count (1 mm on a metre rule). Fractional = absolute / value; percentage = fractional x 100.
Book length: (33.5 +/- 0.05) - (10.0 +/- 0.05) = (23.5 +/- 0.1) cm. Digital scales: keep a last digit that fluctuates by 1 or 2; a larger fluctuation means it is not significant.
